segments.text: Sensation begins when sensory receptors respond to physical energy such as light, sound or pressure. Perception is the brain’s organization and interpretation of that sensory information. A simple formula is: sensation receives information; perception makes sense of it.

This topic becomes easy when studied visually. Instead of memorizing long paragraphs, use diagrams and familiar examples such as seeing a distant object, recognizing a face, or misjudging an illusion.

items.text: Sensory process

: Sense organs convert physical stimulation into neural signals. The exact details differ across vision, hearing, smell, taste and touch, but the general idea is reception, conversion and transmission of information.
Perception
: Perception is active and constructive. Attention, expectations, context, past experience and the properties of the stimulus can influence what a person perceives.
Gestalt principles
: Gestalt psychology shows that people tend to organize visual information into meaningful patterns. Common principles include figure-ground, proximity, similarity, continuity and closure.
Depth cues

: Binocular cues depend on information from both eyes, while monocular cues can operate with one eye. Monocular examples include relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient and motion-related information.
Illusions
: Illusions are systematic differences between physical stimulus conditions and perception. They are useful because they reveal the rules and assumptions used by the perceptual system.
Extra-sensory perception

: ESP appears in the official syllabus as a topic. It should be discussed carefully as a claim investigated in psychology, not presented as an established fact when reliable scientific evidence is lacking.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

blocks.text: From physical energy to psychological experience

items.text: Sensation
: Sensation begins when specialized receptors respond to physical energy such as light, sound waves, pressure or chemical molecules. Sensory systems transduce this energy into neural signals.
Perception
: Perception organizes and interprets sensory information. It is therefore an active inference process: the brain combines current input with context, prior knowledge, attention and expectations.
Absolute threshold

: An absolute threshold is commonly defined as the intensity detected about half the time under specified conditions. Detection is probabilistic because internal noise, attention and expectations vary.
Difference threshold

: The just noticeable difference is the smallest change in stimulation that can be reliably detected. Weber's law captures the useful idea that sensitivity often depends on proportional rather than fixed physical change.
Signal detection

: Signal detection theory separates sensory sensitivity from response criterion. A person may become more willing to say 'yes, I detected it' without the sensory system itself becoming more sensitive.

blocks.text: Vision and hearing as examples of sensory processing

items.text: Vision

: Light enters the eye, is focused on the retina and is transduced by photoreceptors. Rods are highly sensitive in dim conditions, while cones support colour vision and fine detail. Visual information is processed through multiple pathways before conscious perception emerges.
Hearing

: Sound waves cause mechanical movement in the ear that is transformed into neural signals in the cochlea. Frequency is strongly related to perceived pitch, while amplitude contributes to perceived loudness.
Other senses

: Smell and taste rely on chemical receptors; touch includes pressure, temperature and pain-related systems; vestibular and proprioceptive systems provide information about balance and body position. Perception is therefore much wider than sight.
Figure-ground
: The visual system separates a focal object from its background. Ambiguous figures show that the same physical pattern can support more than one organization.
Proximity and similarity
: Elements close together or sharing features are often grouped. These principles reveal that perception imposes organization rather than recording each stimulus independently.
Closure and continuity
: The visual system tends to complete incomplete forms and favour smooth continuous patterns. This helps rapid interpretation in ordinary environments.
Binocular cues
: Retinal disparity and convergence use information from both eyes and are especially helpful for nearby depth judgments.
Monocular cues
: Relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, shading and motion information can support depth judgments with one eye.

segments.text: Bottom-up processing begins with stimulus features and builds toward recognition. Top-down processing uses expectations, context and prior knowledge to interpret incomplete or ambiguous input. Most ordinary perception combines both. Reading poor handwriting is a simple example: visual features matter, but sentence context strongly constrains what the letters are likely to be.

Attention also shapes perception. People cannot process all available input equally, and inattentional blindness demonstrates that visible information can be missed when attention is strongly focused elsewhere. This does not mean the eyes failed; it shows that conscious perception depends on selective processing.

blocks.text: Illusions and claims of extra-sensory perception

items.text: Illusions

: Visual illusions are valuable because they expose normal perceptual assumptions. They should not be treated as proof that perception is generally unreliable; the same shortcuts that create an illusion in a special display often support efficient perception in everyday settings.
Extra-sensory perception

: Claims such as telepathy, clairvoyance and precognition have been investigated experimentally. The appropriate scientific position is to distinguish the existence of claims from the existence of reliable, replicable evidence. Mainstream psychology does not treat ESP as an established sensory system because robust evidence under controlled, reproducible conditions has not been demonstrated.

rows: Avoid this error Do not define perception as merely “seeing.” Perception applies to all sensory systems and includes organization and interpretation.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define sensation and perception, explain the sensory-to-perceptual flow, add Gestalt organization, depth cues and illusions, then discuss determinants of perception with a balanced note on ESP.
• Sensation and perception are connected but not identical.
• Perception organizes and interprets sensory input.
• Depth can be judged using both binocular and monocular cues.
• Illusions demonstrate that perception is constructed, not a perfect camera-like copy.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
